description: How ammonia is made on a huge scale and the trade-offs involved.
content_html:
Reversible Reactions and Dynamic Equilibrium

Some reactions are reversible — the products can re-form the original reactants. Reversible reactions are shown with a double arrow (\ (\rightleftharpoons\)). A simple example is the thermal decomposition and reformation of ammonium chloride:

$$NH_4Cl \rightleftharpoons NH_3 + HCl$$

When heated, ammonium chloride decomposes; when cooled, the gases recombine. In a closed system (where nothing enters or leaves), a reversible reaction eventually reaches dynamic equilibrium. At this point:

  • The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.
  • The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant (but are not necessarily equal).
  • The reaction has not stopped — both directions are still occurring simultaneously.
Key Fact

Dynamic equilibrium: forward and reverse rates are equal; concentrations are constant but not equal to each other. In a reversible reaction, if the forward direction is exothermic, the reverse is endothermic by exactly the same amount of energy.

Le Chatelier’s Principle

Le Chatelier’s principle predicts how equilibrium responds to changing conditions. If you disturb a system at equilibrium, it shifts to counteract that change:

  • Temperature: increasing temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction (to absorb the extra heat). Decreasing temperature shifts it in the exothermic direction.
  • Concentration: increasing the concentration of a reactant shifts equilibrium towards the products. Increasing product concentration shifts it towards the reactants.
  • Pressure (gases only): increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas.

A catalyst does not shift the equilibrium position. It speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached more quickly but the yield at equilibrium is unchanged.

The Haber Process

The Haber process manufactures ammonia (\ (NH_3\)) on an industrial scale. Ammonia is the starting material for fertilisers, nitric acid, and many other chemicals. Without fertilisers, global food production could not support the current world population. The equation is:

$$N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3 \quad \Delta H = \text{exothermic}$$

The raw materials are: nitrogen from fractional distillation of liquid air, and hydrogen from the reaction of natural gas (methane) with steam.

Key Fact

Haber process conditions: approximately 450°C, approximately 200 atmospheres pressure, iron catalyst. The equation is \(N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3\) (exothermic forward reaction). Unreacted gases are recycled.

Compromise Conditions — Why These Values?

The Haber process involves deliberate trade-offs between rate and yield. Understanding these trade-offs is the core of this lesson.

The forward reaction (making ammonia) is exothermic. By Le Chatelier’s principle, a lower temperature favours the exothermic forward direction and gives a higher equilibrium yield of ammonia. However, at low temperatures the rate of reaction is also very slow — it would take a very long time to produce economically useful amounts. A higher temperature increases rate but decreases yield. Around 450°C is a compromise: fast enough to be practical, but not so hot that the yield drops too low to be profitable.

The left side of the equation has 4 moles of gas (\ (N_2 + 3H_2\)) and the right side has 2 moles (\ (2NH_3\)). By Le Chatelier’s principle, higher pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas — the right side, producing more ammonia. In theory, the higher the pressure, the better the yield. However, very high pressures require expensive, reinforced equipment and are costly to maintain and dangerous to run. About 200 atmospheres is again a compromise: it gives a good yield without making the plant uneconomically expensive to build and operate.

An iron catalyst is used to speed up both the forward and reverse reactions, allowing equilibrium to be reached more quickly. The catalyst does not change the equilibrium position or the yield — it only reduces the time needed to get there. Because the yield at equilibrium is around 15–25% under these conditions, the ammonia is continuously removed by cooling and condensing it to a liquid. The unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen gases are recycled back into the reaction vessel. Recycling ensures raw materials are not wasted and the overall yield of the process is much higher than the equilibrium yield suggests.

Why Ammonia Matters: Fertilisers

Most ammonia produced by the Haber process is converted into fertilisers such as ammonium nitrate and ammonium sulfate. Nitrogen is an essential element for plant growth — it is needed to make amino acids, proteins, and DNA. Without synthetic fertilisers, crop yields would be far lower and food would be more expensive or scarce. However, if fertilisers wash off fields into rivers and lakes, they can cause eutrophication — excessive algal growth that depletes oxygen in the water, harming fish and other aquatic life.

The Haber Process as a Science-Society Decision

The Haber process is a compelling example of how industrial chemistry involves decisions that go beyond pure science. The compromise conditions chosen (temperature, pressure, catalyst) are not determined by the chemistry alone — they reflect the balance between what is chemically optimal and what is economically and technically feasible. Building and maintaining pressure vessels safe to operate at very high pressures is expensive. Running processes at very high temperatures consumes large amounts of energy, contributing to operating costs and carbon emissions.

Modern industrial ammonia production continues to evolve. Researchers are investigating lower-temperature, lower-pressure catalytic routes (sometimes called “green ammonia” pathways) that could reduce energy demands and allow ammonia synthesis to be powered by renewable electricity. This illustrates a recurring theme in applied science: the conditions chosen today are not necessarily permanent — they reflect the best available technology at a given time, and new evidence or new materials can change the picture. Evaluating these developments requires weighing evidence about cost, feasibility, and environmental impact together.
exam_tip_html: This topic is heavily tested through “explain the choice of conditions” questions. Always address both rate and yield for temperature and pressure — never say “higher temperature increases yield” (it does the opposite for an exothermic reaction). For pressure: always state that the left side has 4 moles of gas and the right has 2, then apply Le Chatelier’s principle. Do not invent specific percentage yields for the Haber process — the exact figure at equilibrium varies with conditions; describe it as a “moderate yield” which is improved by recycling unreacted gases.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • At dynamic equilibrium, forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations are constant. Le Chatelier’s principle predicts the direction of shift when temperature, concentration, or pressure is changed.
  • The Haber process (\(N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3\)) uses approximately 450°C, approximately 200 atm, and an iron catalyst — all chosen as compromises between rate and yield. Unreacted gases are recycled to maximise overall output.
  • The compromise conditions reflect economic and technical constraints as much as chemistry. Ongoing research into lower-energy ammonia routes illustrates how industrial science evolves as new evidence emerges.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by 'dynamic equilibrium' in a reversible reaction.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction (1); concentrations of reactants and products remain constant, but the reaction has not stopped — both directions are still occurring (1). Secure: both points. Developing: one point only. Emerging: 'forward and reverse reactions happen' without specifying rate equality.

practice_questions.text: The Haber process uses a temperature of approximately 450°C. The forward reaction making ammonia is exothermic. Explain why a lower temperature would give a higher yield but is not used industrially.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: lower temperature favours the exothermic direction by Le Chatelier's principle, increasing equilibrium yield of ammonia (1); however, lower temperature reduces the rate of reaction — it would take too long to produce a useful amount (1); 450°C is a compromise: it gives a reasonable yield with a rate fast enough to be economically viable (1). Secure: three points. Developing: two points. Emerging: one point.

practice_questions.text: The equation for the Haber process is: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Explain why high pressure increases the yield of ammonia, and suggest why a pressure of approximately 200 atmospheres is chosen rather than a much higher pressure.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: there are 4 moles of gas on the left (1 N₂ + 3 H₂) and 2 on the right (2 NH₃) (1); high pressure shifts equilibrium towards fewer moles of gas, i.e. towards the products, increasing yield (1); very high pressures require costly, reinforced equipment and are dangerous to operate (1); 200 atm is a compromise between acceptable yield and manageable cost and safety (1) — 4 marks max. Secure: 3 marks. Developing: 2 marks. Emerging: 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of the iron catalyst in the Haber process. In your answer, state what the catalyst does and does not affect.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: the iron catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions (1); it allows equilibrium to be reached more quickly (1); it does not change the position of equilibrium or the yield — it only reduces the time to reach equilibrium (1). Secure: three points. Developing: two points. Emerging: 'it speeds up the reaction' without addressing equilibrium position.

practice_questions.text: In the Haber process, the yield of ammonia at the operating conditions is moderate. Explain how the industrial process overcomes this limitation to produce ammonia economically.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: the ammonia is continuously removed from the reaction vessel by cooling and condensing it to a liquid (1); removing ammonia shifts the equilibrium to the right to replace it, producing more ammonia (Le Chatelier) (1); unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen gases are recycled back into the reaction vessel (1); this means the raw materials are not wasted (1); over time, the overall yield of the process is much greater than the equilibrium yield suggests (1). Secure: 3–4 points. Developing: 2 points. Emerging: 1 point.

practice_questions.text: Ammonia produced by the Haber process is used to make nitrogen fertilisers. Explain one environmental problem that can arise from the use of nitrogen fertilisers on farmland.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: nitrogen fertilisers can wash off fields into rivers or lakes in rain (1); this causes excessive algal growth (eutrophication) because algae use the extra nitrates as nutrients (1); the algae block light, and when they die, decomposing bacteria deplete oxygen in the water, harming or killing aquatic life (1). Secure: three points. Developing: two points. Emerging: 'causes pollution' without explaining mechanism.

knowledge_checks.q: At dynamic equilibrium in a closed system, which statement is correct?
options: The concentrations of products and reactants are equal
The rate of forward reaction equals the rate of reverse reaction
All reactants have been converted to products

knowledge_checks.q: In the Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, exothermic), which change increases yield?
In the Haber process, unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen gases are _____ back into the reaction vessel to avoid waste.
The Haber process uses an _____ catalyst to speed up the reaction.
Match each Haber process operating condition to its reason.
right: Speeds up reaction without changing equilibrium yield
Compromise between rate (too slow at lower T) and yield (too low at higher T)
Shifts equilibrium towards 2 moles of gas product

flashcard_questions.q: What is the equation for the Haber process?
What are the three operating conditions of the Haber process?
flashcard_questions.a: Approximately 450°C, approximately 200 atmospheres pressure, iron catalyst.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the temperature in the Haber process a compromise?
flashcard_questions.a: Lower temperature gives higher yield but too slow a rate; higher temperature is fast but gives low yield.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does high pressure increase ammonia yield in the Haber process?
flashcard_questions.a: The product side has fewer moles of gas (2 vs 4), so high pressure shifts equilibrium right.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the iron catalyst do in the Haber process?
flashcard_questions.a: It speeds up the reaction so equilibrium is reached faster, without changing the yield.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the Haber process overcome the moderate equilibrium yield?
flashcard_questions.a: Ammonia is condensed out and unreacted gases are recycled.
A state where forward and reverse reaction rates are equal and concentrations remain constant.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Le Chatelier's principle state?
flashcard_questions.a: If equilibrium is disturbed, the system shifts to oppose the change.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the two raw materials for the Haber process and where do they come from?
flashcard_questions.a: Nitrogen from air; hydrogen from methane and steam.

flashcard_questions.q: What environmental problem can nitrogen fertilisers cause if they run off into rivers?
flashcard_questions.a: Eutrophication — excessive algal growth that depletes oxygen and harms aquatic life.

flashcard_questions.q: If the forward reaction in an equilibrium is exothermic, what does increasing temperature do to the yield of products?
flashcard_questions.a: It decreases the yield (equilibrium shifts in the endothermic reverse direction).

glossary_terms.definition: A reaction that can proceed in both the forward direction (reactants to products) and the reverse direction (products back to reactants), shown with the symbol ⇌.
A state in a closed system where the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal and the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
If conditions acting on a system at equilibrium are changed, the position of equilibrium shifts in the direction that opposes the change.
The industrial process for synthesising ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen gases using an iron catalyst, high pressure, and a moderate temperature.
A set of industrial conditions chosen to balance an acceptable reaction rate with an acceptable product yield, rather than optimising either alone.
Substances added to soil to supply nutrients that plants need for growth; nitrogen fertilisers are made from ammonia produced by the Haber process.
